definition: A mode of inference in which a model repeatedly feeds its own intermediate conclusions back as new input, refining them over several passes until it converges on an answer.
details: Instead of committing to a single forward pass, a recurrently reasoning model revisits its thoughts: it drafts, inspects, and revises. Modern reasoning models approximate this with long chains of thought and test-time compute, spending extra tokens to reconsider earlier steps. Quiet-STaR showed that models can learn to think before speaking by generating and reflecting on rationales token by token — a form of recurrent, self-guided reasoning.

explainer.lead: Recurrent reasoning is inference where a model feeds its intermediate conclusions back as new input, refining over several passes until it converges. It matters because it trades extra computation for reconsideration of earlier steps.

tiers.eli5: Like drafting an answer, reading it back, and fixing it before handing it in.
tiers.practitioner: Modern reasoning models approximate it with long chains of thought and test-time compute, spending extra tokens to revisit steps. A pitfall is spending tokens on revision without actually improving the answer.
tiers.paperLevel: A model repeatedly feeds its own intermediate conclusions back as input, refining them across passes until convergence. Quiet-STaR showed models can learn to think before speaking by generating and reflecting on rationales token by token.

explainer.example: A reasoning model drafts a solution, inspects it in its chain of thought, and revises an earlier step before giving the answer.

citation.title: Quiet-STaR: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Think Before Speaking
